title: System Landscapes, Clients, and Project Roles

sections.title: What is an SAP System?
sections.text:
In everyday language, people often say “the SAP system” as if there is just one. In
real projects, there are multiple systems, each serving a different purpose.
An SAP system is a technical environment where SAP software is installed and
runs, with its own database, configuration, and users. From a functional
perspective, you can think of it as:

SAP landscapes are designed this way to ensure that changes are tested
thoroughly before they impact real business operations.
A space where configuration, master data, and
transactional data live.
A place where users log in, run processes, and
test or execute business scenarios.
A stage in the overall lifecycle: learning,
development, testing, or live operations.

sections.title: Typical SAP System Landscape for Projects
sections.text:
Most SAP implementations follow a multi-system landscape. The details vary by
customer, but a common pattern looks like this:
DEV (Development system)
Purpose: Configuration, customization, and unit testing.
Who uses it: Functional consultants, technical consultants, sometimes key
users for early validation.
Key idea: This is where new ideas and changes are built and adjusted.

Purpose Who uses it Key idea

QAS / QA / TEST (Quality or Test system)
Purpose: Integration testing, user acceptance testing (UAT), training, and
sometimes performance testing.
Who uses it: Functional consultants, key users, testers, sometimes end users
involved in UAT.
Key idea: This is where end-to-end processes are validated before going live.

Purpose Who uses it Key idea

PRD (Production system)
Purpose: Live business operations.
Who uses it: Business end users performing daily activities; consultants
usually have limited access, often only for support.
Key idea: This is the “real world” – mistakes here have direct business impact.

Purpose Who uses it Key idea

In addition, many organizations maintain:
Sandbox system
A playground environment for experiments, early evaluations, and proof-of-
concept work.
Often used for trying out ideas without risking formal DEV or QAS.
Training system
A dedicated environment with stable setup and sample data for training end
users and new joiners.
For learners, the important message is: not all SAP screens you see are equal.
Where you log in (DEV vs QAS vs PRD) determines whether you are
experimenting, testing, or working on live business.

sections.title: Why multiple systems are necessary
sections.text:
A single “all-in-one” system would be dangerous. Imagine making configuration
changes directly in the live environment and discovering they break a critical
process. To avoid this, SAP landscapes are separated so that changes are:

Designed and configured in DEV.
Transported and tested in QAS.
Approved and moved to PRD once validated.

This structure:

As an aspiring functional consultant, you should always be aware of which
system you are working in and what that implies for the impact of your actions.
Protects live business from untested changes.
Provides a safe space for learning and trial.
Supports regulatory and audit requirements
(clear separation of duties and change
management).

sections.title: The concept of Client
sections.text:
When logging into SAP, users typically enter:

Many beginners confuse client with system. In SAP terminology, a client is a logical
partition within a single system. You can think of it as:
Separate “logical companies” within one technical installation.
Separate sets of configuration and data, even though they share the same
underlying software.
Client User Password Language

For example, the same DEV system might contain:

The exact setup varies, but the key idea is that client controls which logical
environment you enter. Data and configuration in one client are isolated from
others, which allows:
Different stages (e.g., “golden” config client vs test client).
Different purposes (training vs development) within the same technical
system.
Client 100 – for configuration and
development.
Client 200 – for unit testing.
Client 300 – for training.

For you as a learner:
Always note the client number for exercises and training.
Understand that “wrong client” may mean you cannot see certain data or
configurations.
Recognize that some instructions are client-specific (e.g., “use client 810 for
training”).

sections.title: User Types and Roles in SAP Projects
sections.text:
SAP projects involve many roles. Understanding who does what helps you see
where you fit and what skills you should build.
SAP end user
Focus: Using SAP to perform daily business tasks.
Examples: Accounts payable clerk, sales order processor, warehouse
operator.
Typical responsibilities:

End users do not usually configure the system. They operate within the design
defined by projects and governance.
Deep knowledge of business
processes in their area.
Supporting requirement
discussions and validations.
Participating in testing
and user training.
Acting as champions for
change.

Key user/power user/business process owner
Focus: Bridge between business operations and the SAP project team.
Typical responsibilities:

Key users are critical in workshops and UAT because they understand both the
system and the business context.
Deep knowledge of business processes in
their area
Supporting requirement discussions and
validations
Participating in testing and user training
Acting as champions for change

Functional consultant
Focus: Process and configuration for a specific area (e.g., FI, MM, SD).
Typical responsibilities:

This is the target role for your program: aspiring SAP S/4HANA functional
consultant.
Understanding business
requirements
Mapping requirements to SAP
standard processes
Configuring settings in SAP
Preparing functional
specifications for technical work
Supporting testing, cutover, and
go-live
Creating documentation and
training material

Technical consultant
Focus: Technical aspects such as development, integration, and system
operations.
Types:

ABAP developer – builds custom programs, interfaces, enhancements.
Integration consultant – handles connections between SAP and other systems.
Basis/technical administrator – manages system performance, upgrades, and
technical configuration.
Security consultant – designs and maintains roles and authorizations.
Functional and technical consultants work closely together. Functional defines the
“what” and “why”; technical implements the “how” at code and infrastructure level.

sections.text:
Your bridge module and the subsequent 12‑week implementation program are

You are not being trained to be an end user who only posts documents.
You are being prepared to:

sections.title: Basics of Access, Login, and Security
sections.text:
Even though detailed security design is handled by specialized teams, every
consultant should understand basic concepts about access.
Login elements
When logging into an SAP system, you typically provide:

Client – which logical environment in the system you are entering.
User ID – your unique account.
Password – your secret authentication key.
Language – which logon language to use for menus and messages.
Different projects and training environments may use different client numbers
and logon details. Always follow the instructions provided for your training or
project.
Client User ID Password Language

Roles and authorizations
In SAP, users do not have unrestricted access to everything. Instead, they are
assigned roles, each containing authorizations that control:
Which transactions or apps they can use.
Which organizational units and data they can access (for example, which
company codes or plants).
Which actions they can perform (display only, create, change, approve).
For security, compliance, and audit reasons, companies separate duties. For
example:
A user who creates purchase orders may not be allowed to approve vendors.
A user who posts payments may not create bank master data.
As a functional consultant:
You need enough access to configure and test your processes in project
systems.
You should also understand that when a user says “I can’t see this app,” it is
often an authorization issue, not a system failure.
